subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext:
I have a question I should like to direct to the Acting Prime Minister. Is it a fact that by a declaration made on August 7, 1953, all 16 allied countries involved in the Korean war are pledged to resist unprovoked aggression
promptly and in unison? If so, what position is now being taken by the Canadian government with respect to the armed seizure on the high seas of the United States ship Pueblo by units of the North Korean navy?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext: I am not in a position to answer the specific question raised by the hon. gentleman but I can say we are following with interest developments in connection with this very serious matter. Communications with our allies continue. This is a matter of great concern directly to the United States because they are the ones involved. They are exercising, I think, caution and restraint in their approach.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext: I realize that the Minister of Transport who is acting as prime minister today might have been taken somewhat unawares by my question, though I did try to give him notice. This is a serious subject and I am wondering whether the Acting Prime Minister might not be in a position later this day to ask the house for leave to revert to motions and make a statement informing us whether or not the government is bound by this declaration, to which we are a party, to come to the aid of the United States or South Korea should further unprovoked hostilities take place, or should the United States attempt to liberate the USS Pueblo.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext:
Even if I were able to get the
information requested during the course of the afternoon I am not sure that I would be in a position to make a statement. This involves, I would suspect, a question of the interpretation of an agreement. I also believe that the allegation that this incident occurred in international waters would be relevant, and I certainly would not wish to express what would amount to a legal opinion on the subject.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext: Is the minister telling the house that the government is not satisfied that this seizure was made in international waters?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext:
No. I said the allegation was made that it was, and that is what I believe to have been the case.

January 25, 1968
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext: As preparation for possible heavy responsibilities in the future, would the Acting Prime Minister not take this opportunity to get some additional information for the house right now before the question period is over, and let the house and the Canadian people know exactly what are the facts about the situation internationally which is, apparently, very grave?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NORTH KOREA-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT IN LIGHT OF INTERCEPTION OF USS "PUEBLO"
speechtext: I would be delighted to give to the hon. gentleman and to the house all possible information, but this is a subject of such magnitude that even if I were to attempt to spend the next few minutes seeking to amplify my own inadequate knowledge I am not sure I could satisfy the hon. gentleman.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the President of the Privy Council with respect to the report of the task force on foreign ownership and control of the Canadian economy. subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Acting Prime Minister. Was the Minister of Finance expressing government policy when he stated in Winnipeg on
January 25, 1968



Friday that Canada must welcome development capital from outside its borders to guarantee the industrialization of much of the country, particularly the west?

subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: I am certain he was speaking on behalf of the government when he said that, Mr. Speaker. I think it is agreed by everyone that we have to have additional assistance, due to our inadequate supply of development capital, but this does not mean that there cannot be room for difference of opinion as to the form the infusion of this capital should take, and that there cannot be room for reasonable argument as to what the rules of engagement should be and the terms under which those using it should be good corporate Canadian citizens.

subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a further supplementary question to the President of the Privy Council. Does he agree with what the Acting Prime Minister has stated is government policy?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a further supplementary question to the President of the Privy Council. He said that the report was to be made public but he did not answer the question as to whether or not, subsequent to making the report public, the government intends to issue a white paper setting forth its views on the matter.

subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: I think the government's views, Mr. Speaker, will become apparent in due course. I am not convinced myself that in addition to making the report public anything much would be gained by spending perhaps another considerable number of months in preparing a white paper. The government's intentions as to future procedure will be made known-

subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: In due course.

subtopic: REPORT OF TASK FORCE RESPECTING FOREIGN OWNERSHIP IN CANADA
speechtext: -will be made known at the time the report is tabled.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct this question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. In order to eliminate existing doubts, will the minister assure the people of the Yukon that the cut-backs, totalling approximately $13 million, of federal government money will be restored to the government of the Yukon forthwith, now that the council has passed the taxing legislation upon which the minister had insisted?

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the so-called cut-backs were the result of repudiation by council of an agreement made here with me. I told them the agreement would become effective on the date when they undertook to respect the agreement they made in Ottawa. They have now done that, so the agreement which we made in respect of funds coming forward from us will date from the day when they accepted their undertaking.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question which is intended for clarification. Are the people of the Yukon then to understand that all the so-called cut-backs will in fact be restored now that the necessary taxing legislation has been passed including the cost sharing program under the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the council of the Yukon is fully aware of the undertaking I

January 25, 1968
Inquiries of the Ministry gave and which, they accepted at that time. I believe they have now agreed, with only one person objecting, that they should have lived up to the agreement they undertook when they were in Ottawa.

I have a further supplementary question. What I am seeking here is an assurance for the people of the territory. All I am asking the minister is whether he can assure the people of the Yukon that the so-called cut-backs, to use his own term, will be restored pursuant to the provision of the agreement, which was met, and now that the council has in fact passed the taxing legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Our agreement stands. We have kept it, and it will date from the time they voted to respect the agreement they made. I believe that was on Monday. subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Following a study by British scientists in London of the Universities Federation for Animal Welfare, a report was issued stating that shotguns, captive bolt pistols and the use of strychnine poison in the killing of seals should be banned, and the shooting of seal pups by rifle from a boat forbidden. In view of the fact that the killing of seals should be done as humanely as possible, did the minister or his officials study the British report before authorizing tests to use a 410 gauge shotgun during the hunting season which opens in March?

subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the report made by the British scientists was studied and I was delighted to see that they are taking practically the same attitude as we are taking here in Canada. With respect to the experiment we will be carrying on during the seal season in March, the Ontario Humane Society has provided us with a different type of weapon. We have agreed to try it on a limited scale and our officials will be accompanied by a veterinarian and by a representative of the
S.P.C.A. during the hunt. We will then be able to determine the effect of such a weapon.

subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES
speechtext:
The minister's announcement stated that the decision to make the tests followed a recent meeting by the department
Inquiries of the Ministry with representatives of the Ontario Humane Society, the Canadian Wildlife Service, the Defence Research Board and the National Research Council. Has the minister consulted with officials of the sealing industry on this matter and will the sealing industry officials be present when the minister's shotgun policy goes into effect?

subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES
speechtext: I do not think it would be right to call it the minister's shotgun policy because the minister is practically convinced that the use of the shotgun will not be too effective in this kind of operation. I thought, however, that it was advisable to try this new type of weapon with limited power as an experiment. The members of the sealing industry are aware of this experiment.

subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES
speechtext: Since it is necessary in the national interest that the highest value for the seal pelts be obtained, will the hit or miss methods practised by seal killers operating from private planes be stopped or regulated?

subtopic: SEALS-USE OF SHOTGUN IN SLAUGHTERING PROCEDURES
speechtext: I think I have already made it clear that it was our intention to control or limit the operation of airplanes during the seal hunt. I would hope that this year no new licences will be issued. Also, due to the fact that the opening of the season is delayed by ten days this by itself will limit the operations by planes.

speechtext:

subtopic: ICEBREAKING OPERATIONS ON ST. LAWRENCE RIVER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ICEBREAKING OPERATIONS ON ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. I would remind the house, with regard to the problem of high-rise buildings, that the national capital and its buildings are welcome in Halifax. I would ask the Acting Prime Minister whether, in light of the increased activity in the middle and upper reaches of the St. Lawrence river up as far as Montreal, he would now give assurance to the ports of Halifax and Saint John that this is indeed for water control purposes and not for economic reasons involving ships of other nations.

subtopic: ICEBREAKING OPERATIONS ON ST. LAWRENCE RIVER

yesterday, it has been a long time since I found myself in a position to agree with anything put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer. However, after ten years in this house I suppose one does mellow somewhat toward those who support other political groups, and after reading his amendment I am prepared to vote for it. I say this because I believe that the words "while ensuring that the most broadly held opinions receive appropriate consideration" and the words "while alert and responsive to public preferences in this and other aspects of programming" serve to strengthen the original clause of the bill.
The government apparently believed that it should include in the bill under the general title of a broadcasting policy for Canada a clause which deals with programming. To those of us who on occasion have an opportunity to watch television, and especially some of the C.B.C. programs, this is understandable. We know that there is a wide variety of opinion regarding what is desirable and acceptable and that this applies to the theatre, to motion pictures, to music and the arts. What is classed as acceptable music by this generation would certainly not have been acceptable only a decade ago. I know the minister will agree with me that Viennese waltzes seem strangely out of place alongside Beatle rhythms. It is therefore evident that tastes, habits and customs change, and a medium like television, which is catering to age groups from the cradle to the grave, is bound to find difficulty in providing a bill of fare that is satisfactory to everyone. It is for these reasons, Mr. Chairman, that I believe we are entitled and are expected to voice our opinions on programming so that those in charge of these matters will be aware of the voice of the people, as it were, expressed through their elected representatives.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The government has suggested that the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should be varied and comprehensive, should provide reasonable opportunity for the expression of conflicting views on matters of public controversy, and that the programming provided by each broadcaster should be of a high standard, using predominantly Canadian creative and other resources. These are good guide lines, Mr. Chairman, and have without doubt been laid down by the government because of difficulties experienced by the C.B.C. management in arranging programs in the past. We would not have such lengthy discussions

in the house or the committee had there not been considerable public discontent about the programs which the C.B.C. has presented in the past. After reading the guide lines I see no reason for rejecting the amendment that the hon. member for Red Deer has moved. I see no reason for rejecting a similar amendment if it informs C.B.C. management what our thoughts, as members of this house, are on that important matter.
A moment ago I spoke of the differences in our society and of the difficulty that is faced by C.B.C. management in preparing a bill of fare that is suitable for everyone. It is crystal clear that we have in Canada differences in languages, customs, tastes, habits, and in age groups. Nevertheless, it is truly amazing to see how similar Canadians of all groups are to people in other parts of the world. For example, applying the golden rule of doing unto others what we would have them do unto us, if we show concern, courtesy, kindliness or anger, sympathy or compassion, each will be returned in kind. Perhaps we ought to put that on the record as a guide line for those who are responsible for the programs.
Had this rule been followed, then surely we should not have been subjected to a parody of God last Sunday evening by a group of paid performers. That type of sick comedy apparently is indicative of the rot which has set in in the C.B.C., as mentioned some time ago by the minister. This type of comedy, in my opinion, is not funny it offends the Christian teaching of thousands of years and can only arouse in those who watch it pity for the producer of sponsor of the program. The estimates for the C.B.C. this year exceed $143 million, an increase of about $29
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting million in one year. Canadians generally, whether they are of French, English, German, Italian, Norwegian, Scottish, Irish or other origins, as a rule want good value for their money. Canadians today are asking themselves, not only with respect to expenditures by C.B.C. but with respect to many other expenditures that are made by this government, are we getting value for our money? If the C.B.C. were operating as a private concern it would have gone broke by now.
When I was first elected in 1957 the C.B.C. was spending more than $52 million a year of the taxpayers' money. I thought then that more than $1 million a week to subsidize this organization was too much to pay. Today the subsidy is almost three times as big. I caution those who are responsible for programming to ask themselves in future: Is this program entertaining, is it acceptable to the Canadian people, as well as: Is it good value for our money, and can we afford it?
I realize that we need creative minds in the C.B.C. That organization has done much that is commendable. I temper that comment with a caution that creativity does not give a programmer the right to be irresponsible, the right to deal in sensationalism or to show programs that are in bad taste. I think a few words will indicate the general trend of some of the speakers in support of the amendment. They want to play down the emphasis on what I will call the kooky people, the far-out fringe. They want to have more emphasis placed on broad opinions generally held by the public and less on the lunatic fringe. They say that on grounds of morality we need to have more emphasis on the respectability of broadcasting and that we want to prevent the appearance of such people as nazis. Those who have been against the amendment have used such phrases as "restrictive amendment," "amounting to censorship," "trying to destroy freedom," "conformist amendment." On the one hand, we have those people who feel that the respectability of Canadian viewers and their sense of what is moral and decent are outraged too often by certain programs that are presented. On the other hand, those against the amendment have taken the stand that anyone who wants to protect people from this sort of thing is simply protectionist and is restricting freedom. Obviously, Mr. Chairman, there is a little bit of truth on both sides.
Any time we suggest that parliament should give a directive to our national broadcasting system as to the type of programming we would prefer we can say that by the weight of the opinion of parliament we are trying to censor and restrict freedom of choice to some extent. However, there is no such thing as black and white. There is, of course, a middle ground in this matter and, on the basis of the remarks made by various speakers as well as my own opinion, I really feel that what is irksome to most people is the tremendous impact made by so many far-out programs. The fact is that one or two programs have been so very unacceptable that the shock of that sort of thing has made members forget how many programs do conform to the ordinary respectability and moral sense of the citizens of Canada.

DEBATES	January 25, 1968
I have often thought about the line of censorship that broadcasters should use to guide themselves lest they use the airwaves in a distasteful manner. As an ordinary citizen this is my feeling on the matter. If over that medium of entertainment during the late hours of the evening there comes a program in which the subject is handled in such a way that myself, my wife and a group of rather sophisticated friends watching it would feel shocked and offended if any of our group used such language or talked in such a manner as on the television program, then in my view that program is not very fit entertainment for a group of sophisticated people. If it is too lewd or disreputable for sophisticated, broadminded people, and I think I am pretty broadminded, then we must look closely at the reasons for presenting that program. Are they crusading for something? Is it necessary public instruction? If it is necessary public instruction, is this the proper medium for that public instruction? Obviously on some of these grounds we cannot justify some of these programs.
I think one of the difficulties is that broadcasting and success in broadcasting are in some respects like politics. The more publicity you get and the greater the sensation you create the bigger your name is. This seems to be the badge of success in that medium to some extent.
I am the last one in this chamber to want to add any form of censorship. I think that the aim of this bill should not be compulsory but advisory in this regard, and I feel that the present wording of the clause goes about as far as we can in this regard when it refers to conflicting views on matters of public controversy. Surely that is not, as the mover of the amendment seems to feel a suggestion that the medium should be used to raise public controversy, to try to bring something out of an obscure dark room that nobody is thinking about and have it discussed and raised in a manner that offends the sensibilities of many Canadians.
I do not think there can be any complete directive on this matter of public controversy. As well as offering entertainment television is a news medium. If a subject is of any importance to the nation and has an impact on our economic or cultural life, television should not miss an opportunity to bring as many aspects of the situation as possible to the attention of the public. I do not think it would cost any money or offend any broadcaster's sense of duty to find a way to do this
January 25, 1968	COMMONS DEBATES	5953
in good taste, if it can possibly be done that way.
As a lawyer I am concerned about the concept of trying, in a statute of this kind, to direct the method in which judgment shall be used by a regulatory body. Frankly, I do not think it is possible. When we as legislators are trying to draft an act we sometimes try to do so with such preciseness that we will know in advance the way in which a court is going to interpret it so as to give full effect to what we mean, but one of our difficulties is that we are not clear in our own minds what we mean. We have only vague ideas and therefore we only convey our ideas vaguely.
However, one hon. member put his finger on a solution to the problem when he said that the people who are making these regulations and running our broadcasting systems have access to Hansard. They are able to read for themselves what has been said and to gain a consensus of opinion, if they can, from the remarks made in this chamber. This certainly is not a method open to the courts that can be used in trying to arrive at a strict interpretation of what parliament meant. But here, as I have suggested, we cannot give a strict interpretation to what we mean because the meaning is vague. The meaning is different for each one of us. Rene Tremblay who was a friend of mine. If I had been advised this morning, when I asked if the broadcasting bill would

DEBATES	January 25, 1968
be before the committee today, that there would not be a vote this afternoon, I would have attended the funeral. But I was told we would be debating the bill, which answer kept me in Ottawa because I understood we would be referring back to subclause (c). Not until this afternoon, after I had given up my reserved seat on the bus and plane did I learn that no vote was coming forward. Therefore I cannot be accused of continuing the discussion in order to postpone the vote at this time.
This debate gives me the opportunity of discussing the necessity of this amendment and other amendments to provide guide lines for the operation of our national television and radio networks. I do not believe we could have had more concise or blatant examples of the need for guide lines for conducting programming on both public and private networks than those examples we had last night and again this afternoon. I sat in this house and witnessed both episodes.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We have rules of debate which are summed up in the standing orders of the House of Commons. Standing order 35 reads as follows:
No member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty, nor of any of the royal family, nor of His Excellency or the person administering the government of Canada: nor use offensive words against either house, or against any member thereof. No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
Why do we have these rules of debate if it is not necessary to have guide lines? Although we have these rules of debate, little attention is paid to them. I was very provoked last night by the personal attack made by a member of this house against the hon. member for Roberval. I went across the floor of the house and pointed out to the hon. member for Roberval that standing order 35 provides that no member shall use offensive words against any member of either house. If I ever heard offensive words being used against a member of this house, last night was a prime example.
I do not like to see one person talking down to another, and I do not like to see one person setting himself up as a judge to evaluate the opinions of another member of the house who has been duly and properly elected by the constituency of Roberval and has every right to express his opinions whether or not any member of the house thinks he does not know what he is talking about. I

I would like at this time to refer to a report that appears in this morning's Globe and Mail. Of course, there seem to be many lovers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation who seem to have the conviction that nothing wrong can be done by the C.B.C. and that it is the proper measuring stick for all other sources of information. I had intended during the question period this afternoon to ask the Secretary of State whether we have to rely on reports of the Associated Press and Southam News Service for details of what is going on in North Korea, where a United States warship has been impounded by the North Korean people.
Has the C.B.C. yet sent camera crews, observers and commentators off to North Korea with the attitude, to hell with the expense, let us get the facts for the C.B.C.? Or do we have to rely on Southam News Service, the Associated Press and the Canadian Press for details upon which to form an opinion of this action? I refer to the C.B.C. news coverage because I wish to quote from the evidence given yesterday at a formal, government hearing in Cayuga, the county seat of Haldimand county, Ontario. This hearing was conducted under the direction of the provincial government of Ontario.
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting
The report to which I refer appears on the front page of this morning's Globe and Mail. It is a very detailed report. I wonder whether a report over the C.B.C. news service, either radio or television, will be given in such detail as it is printed in the fourth estate. Yesterday was the second or third day of a hearing which is investigating whether farmers and cattle in the Dunnville area are dying from fluoride poisoning, as alleged on a C.B.C. documentary some time ago. This documentary, of course, was fully paid for by the Canadian taxpayers.
May I leave that subject for a moment, Mr. Chairman, in order to refer to the recent remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South in which he referred to the remarks of the hon. member for Timmins who stated that if you did not like a program you could always turn it oil. I later made the comment to my good friend the hon. member for Timmins that it would be satisfactory to me if you could turn the program off and your taxes stopped running. But when you turn a C.B.C. program off your taxes keep on running and you are paying for the blather that is coming over the air whether or not you want to hear it or look at it. While we may be able to turn our radio or television off, do not forget that our taxes keep on running and we are paying for the program just the same.
One of the witnesses who appeared before the commission appointed by the Ontario government to inquire into the ridiculous allegations made on the C.B.C. so-called documentary "Air of Death" was Dr. F. Graham Marson of Hamilton, Ontario. Dr. Marson was on the stand in Cayuga yesterday. I presume he was sworn and was under oath, because it is a commission investigation under the direction of the department of health of the Ontario provincial government. Dr. Marson, who has been a consultant for Dunnville area doctors since 1958, said he was unable to find any evidence of fluoride poisoning during his examinations of two farmers concerned. He is a specialist in internal medicine and was called in by Dunnville doctors to examine two farmers suspected of suffering fluoride poisoning. He described the television program "Air of Death" as disgusting nonsense that left him questioning the credibility of any C.B.C. documentary.
When you have a man of the standing of Dr. Graham Marson of Hamilton in his community and profession referring to a so-called documentary on the C.B.C. as disgusting nonsense that left him questioning the credibility

Canadian Policy on Broadcasting of any C.B.C. documentary, I would say that we certainly need more guide lines for the direction of C.B.C. program directors than we have at the moment, because they are able to put programs like that on the air despite the so-called controls that are supposed to apply to them.
Dr. Marson pointed out under oath yesterday that his diagnosis of Jacob Vanderbeek, 68, in 1965, and Joseph Casina, 55, last July, was confirmed by intensive examinations last November at Toronto General hospital. The newspaper report goes on to say:
Dr. K. J. R. Wightman, physician in chief at Toronto General, told the inquiry that the two men were examined over a period of three or four weeks after the inquiry was ordered.
He said no evidence was found that the two men were suffering from fluoride poisoning.
You may wonder whether I have any personal knowledge of this documentary and the results that have flowed from the false statements that were made on the C.B.C. program.
I point out that about 48 hours after these allegations came pouring over the air on a C.B.C. program my daughter, who is a student at the University of Ottawa, came to me and stated that she had been approached by the private television network, C.T.V., to go on the air in a discussion on pollution. I said to her, "Young lady, I wonder how they came to pick on you, with the thousands of students at the University of Ottawa." She said, "I don't know, dad, but there are going to be three students from the University of Carle-ton and three from the University of Ottawa, and we are supposed to take part in a panel discussion with the federal minister of health, Mr. MacEachen." I said to her, "Well, it is interesting to me that they have asked you, Margaret. But what is it you would like?" She said, "I want to know if there is any body in the charges that have been made over the C.B.C. network, to start with, and I would like to know if they should be refuted or supported." I said to my daughter, in regard to her preparation for the C.T.V. program, "This is not a matter of federal concern, it is a provincial matter," and I got her the necessary portions of the law in question on the pollution of air and water.
I wish at this time to thank my friend the hon. member for Nickel Belt to whom I went for the supporting evidence to give my daughter. I went to him because I know the arguments that have been going on in the Nickel Belt-Sudbury area for the past 50 years over the question of pollution of the air and water there from the mining of nickel.

DEBATES	January 25, 1968
The hon. member for Nickel Belt gave me a tremendous file of facts and figures based upon investigations over the years by labour unions, government authorities and doctors in regard to this matter.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I turned the material over to the students of the University of Ottawa and they went to the studio with the Minister of National Health and Welfare. A half hour program was presented in which the private network showed the public of Canada that this matter was not a federal responsibility and that if there was a responsibility for the illness of two men and the deaths of animals it was a provincial one. The fact that the province of Ontario has appointed a commission to investigate the matter shows that they accept the responsibility. However, why was there an unnecessary hubbub raised that the federal government was at fault in the matter? The reason for it was that a federal crown agency, the C.B.C., had put a program on the air which was fictitious and false from start to finish.
I will continue with the remarks made yesterday by Dr. Marson. Dr. Marson described as "complete imagination and fabrication" the statements made by Mr. Casina on the C.B.C. television program that he, Dr. Marson, had said Mr. Casina was "the third known case in North America". Dr. Marson said in his evidence yesterday "having never heard of a fluorisis case in Canada or the United States, I know jolly well I did not say that." Then Dr. Marson told the public inquiry that he was disgusted at the fact that the C.B.C. did not get in touch with him before the program was broadcast to check the statements attributed to him by farmers who took part in the show. He then made the following amazing statement: "I think it is disgusting that Stanley Burke does not ring me up before the program but does the following Wednesday."
In introducing his amendment to subclause (d) the hon. member for Red Deer referred to the fact that it was a carryover from subclause 2 (c). I hope I may be allowed to read subclause 2 (c). It reads as follows:
(c) all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for programs they broadcast but the right to freedom of expression, subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations-
The hon. member for Red Deer wants to put a little more teeth into subclause 2 (d), following the reference that is made to generally applicable statutes and regulations in
January 25, 1968

subclause 2 (c). Surely adherence to the truth might be one of the regulations that could be observed by the C.B.C. in its programming.
When Dr. Marson pointed out that the statements attributed to him by a farmer were false and that the only time he was consulted with regard to the validity of these remarks was after the program rather than before it, he was giving evidence that the C.B.C. themselves admit that something was mishandled when they put that program on the air.
To show how much Dr. George L. Waldbott of Detroit knew about the subject, Drs. Wightman and Marson were cross-examined by the commission counsel, Mr. Rodger Gordon. Mr. Gordon told the investigation at Cayuga that Dr. Waldbott had been invited to testify. Mr. Gordon read a letter he received from Dr. Waldbott saying he would be glad to testify but that at present his data is incomplete. It was on January 24 that Mr. Gordon, the commission counsel, read the letter from Dr. Waldbott.
Although Dr. Waldbott stated his data was incomplete, it did not stop him from making allegations and charges that the province of Ontario is spending money to prove unfounded and it did not stop the C.B.C. putting the program on the air some time ago. Dr. Waldbott then said he would like to see the reports on the examinations at the Toronto General hospital. I quote from Dr. Waldbott's letter the following sentence:
This would make it possible for me to render a valid assessment of their illness.
I wonder what kind of assessment he made of their illness before, if he now admits that he has not seen the results of the investigation made by the Toronto General hospital under the direction of the department of health of the province of Ontario and at the expense of the taxpayers of Ontario because of false accusations put on the air by the C.B.C. He said that if he was allowed to see the results of the investigation made at the Toronto General hospital he would be able to give a valid assessment of their condition. Certainly this is a backhanded way of admitting that the first assessment made by Dr. Waldbott was invalid and should not have been on the air.
To show the expense to which the taxpayers of Ontario are being put by these false accusations made on the air on a C.B.C. program under the few guide lines they have now, I point out that Mr. Gordon, the commission counsel, told one of the farmers who
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting was complaining he was affected by fluoride fumes from polluted air that he and his wife could make arrangements to enter the Toronto General hospital if they felt they were suffering from fluoride poisoning and their expenses would be paid by the province of Ontario.
When the province of Ontario pays expenses it means that the taxpayers of Ontario are paying them, and this is a heavy expense which is being forced on the people of Ontario through false accusations which went out over the airwaves on a C.B.C. so-called documentary. No wonder Dr. Marson said that the falsity of one documentary casts doubts on all other C.B.C. documentaries.
I strongly support the amendment of the hon. member for Red Deer who is trying to put more teeth into this clause which endeavours to control programming in the public and private sectors of both the radio and television world, and I call upon all other members of the house to do the same, particularly after hearing this concrete example of irresponsible documentation by the C.B.C. as testified to by Dr. F. Graham Marson, an outstanding specialist in internal medicine, and Dr. K. J. R. Wightman, physician in chief at the Toronto General hospital, as recently as yesterday.

Mr. Chairman, subclause (e) of clause 2 is a source of great puzzlement to me, by reason of its evasive wording, which reads thus:
All Canadians are entitled to broadcasting service in English and French as public funds become available;
Mr. Chairman, I think this is the worst excuse ever found not to proceed immediately with the building of relay stations to complete the French network of the C.B.C. It is quite easy and inexpensive to set up, in the large urban centers of the country, relay stations which would allow the French language to be heard and listened to throughout Canada, without prejudice to anyone and without disturbing anyone's habits.
A few million dollars would be enough to carry out this project which, besides, is consistent with the basic aims of state-owned radio. I feel that, in this way, the federal government would make a major contribution to the solution of the problem of national unity, would prevent too often heard recriminations, perhaps, and would also enable those who believe in Canada to assert that federal organizations contribute perhaps more than the province of Quebec to the development of French culture.
I become very sceptical when I am told:
-as public funds become available;
It would be very easy to have an investigation conducted by auditors, accountants or administrators in order to prove that the C.B.C. never has much scruples about spending public funds. That is an open secret, for we all know that a considerable amount of money is being spent and that this could be

prevented through normal and not even overly strict control. I could talk on this subject at great length.
Mr. Chairman, I will give several examples to support the assertions I have made this afternoon. Let us take the case of television in Quebec. There are two television stations in Quebec city which are controlled, owned and operated by essentially Canadian interests; these are channels 4 and 5. The two private stations in Quebec, which broadcast local programs for 40 hours a week, are operated by a staff of 130. In other words, 130 people manage to operate two private television stations in Quebec city, and their local weekly broadcasting output is 40 hours.
On the other hand, channel 11 of the C.B.C. which provides a local production of seven hours a week, compared to 40 hours for private stations, employs 200 people compared to 130 working for two stations owned and operated by private enterprise.
That is merely a small example of the expenses which I could qualify as orgiac, excessive and unjustified, which the C.B.C. makes out of the public moneys without any scruples, without any control, which should normally be exercised by responsible and competent directors, concerned with public integrity.
Mr. Chairman, we could multiply the examples and prove easily that the situation which exists in Quebec city also exists throughout the country. It is clear and obvious that private enterprise operates much more efficiently with fewer people, a lower budget and a higher viewers' rating.
We are called upon to vote estimates for the C.B.C. which has yet to show that it is desirous to avoid unnecessary expenditures. Under the circumstances, I have the right to say that the funds are available if we are willing to exercise a tighter control over C.B.C. expenditures. The four or five million dollars we would need to spread the French culture and the French language throughout Canada, without hurting anyone, without restricting anyone's freedoms, are available.
We would have the money available and I wonder if it would not be possible to proceed with this inquiry to allow such easy savings to enable us to build in the large centres of the country relay stations of the French network of the C.B.C., so that French-speaking communities could follow the events and obtain information in their own language.

Mr. Chairman, I made a few remarks and I shall close quickly to bring to the attention of the house that there are exorbitant expenditures in the C.B.C. No one will question the basis of such a statement. I have cited clearly the case of two private television stations in the city of Quebec operated by private enterprise. These two stations have a much higher rating than that of the C.B.C. with a personnel of only 130 employees. On the other hand, the C.B.C. has only one television station in Quebec and 200 employees.
That is the situation in the city of Quebec. Whereas the two private stations supply 40 hours a week of programming, the C.B.C. supplies seven hours a week: 200 employees for seven hours of production against 130 for 40 hours of production. That the C.B.C. should pay a correspondent such as Mr. Jean-Marc Poliquin, a correspondent such as Mr. Pierre Sauve, I am in full accord, because they are two competent and serious newspapermen who deserve adequate fees.
But if, on the other hand, the C.B.C. is involved in such patronage as the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) has mentioned, it is not surprising that the same faces are always seen on certain programs. For instance, what fees are paid to the participants in Quiz programs?
Besides, those people would be glad to appear on television for the mere sake of being seen and would perhaps refuse any fee, but in addition to gratifying their personal vanity, they are paid fantastic fees to take part in certain programs.
Who can tell us, for instance, how much is paid Gilles Pellerin's guest to appear on the program where one must not say yes or no? This requires exceptional talent. The thing is to be present and never say yes or no. All kinds of questions are asked. How much are paid the participants in such programs? Does it really requil'e any exceptional talent to perform the feat of not saying yes or no during 60 or 100 seconds? The participants are probably paid $100 or $200, while some humble labourers or farmers work 16 hours a day to earn $10 or $12. Then, we have the right, as representatives of the people, to insist upon a certain control. I do not think it is exaggerating to do so.
Why do I ask for such a control? It is because I am convinced that if an accountant or an auditor, who has the necessary experience, would make a point of investigating thoroughly the expenses of the C.B.C., we would surely be able to save the five millions of dollars necessary to set up relay stations allowing the French language to be heard throughout Canada. All that is necessary is to build stations retransmitting programs of the French network of the C.B.C. in large English-speaking centres in the country, to spread from coast to coast the French fact so as to meet the views expressed in the Laurendeau-Dun-ton report, and sanction the official recognition of the two languages in the country. Secretary of State, who is piloting this bill at the present time, made the statement in the House of Commons directly to the hon. member for Lapointe that this is a declaratory clause and "we have tried to use appropriate language throughout". Well, the statement that this entire policy clause, clause 2, is a declaratory clause is borne out by the fact that we have

The use of the word "declaratory" is, as the hon. member for Lotbiniere has already pointed out, an indication that this is a promise without immediate substance. He points out that we may have to wait a considerable length of time before any action is taken under such a phrase as "all Canadians are entitled to be given service in English and French as public funds become available".
Of course, a declaratory clause may not bind the cabinet to any definite action. It does not necessarily bind the radio and television world to certain action so long as it is considered to be declaratory. But I can assure you that it would not be very long, if such a bill were passed, until we would be hearing the term used that parliament had given a mandate that all Canadians are entitled to a broadcasting service in English and in French as public funds become available. We have heard the term, "the C.B.C. mandate," for the past 20 years. There never was a mandate given to the C.B.C., but in their annual reports they always refer to a mandate. The proof of the pudding lies in the fact that when this bill was introduced in October the Secretary of State pointed out that this was the first mandate "we have drawn up for the C.B.C.". If a bill introduced in October 1967 was the first mandate drawn up for the C.B.C, what was the idea of referring annually to the mandate of the C.B.C from about 1940 to 1967. There was and is no mandate, yet the term is used "mandate for the C.B.C.".
One can imagine what will happen if clause 2 (e) passes since it declares that all Canadians are entitled to broadcasting service in English and French as public funds become available. Despite the fact that we have the statement of the Secretary of State of December 21 that this is a declaratory clause "and we have tried to use appropriate language throughout", as I said before if we pass it, we will be saddled for the rest of time with the accusation that it is a mandate about which parliament is doing nothing. The interesting phrase "as public funds become available", as the hon. member for Lotbiniere has indicated, can only tease those who are very anxious to have the use of French spread throughout Canada from coast to coast which would cost the taxpayers of Canada millions and millions of dollars for C.B.C. hardware. I do not intend to make any remarks that would tend to bring to a head the situation which exists in this dominion with regard to the two languages, one of which is official throughout

Canada while the second may be used in the province of Quebec and in the houses of parliament.

I should like to draw the attention of our French-speaking compatriots-I dislike very much the expression "French Canadian" and much prefer the expression "French speaking Canadian"-to the fact that Canada lies within the province of a division made by Pope Alexander VI at Rome in 1493 in which he gave this part of the world to Spain. We are all aware that Columbus discovered America in 1492, but very few people seem to know that in 1493 His Holiness Pope Alexander VI of the Roman Catholic church divided the unknown world of the west between Spain and Portugal.
For Canadians the interesting point is that Canada, at the north end of America, was given to Spain by a papal bull issued on May 3, 1493. There was another papal bull issued on May 4, 1493. The reason behind the two bulls was that Columbus returned to Europe and announced his discovery of the Indies to the king of Spain. The King of Portugal maintained that he only discovered islands that had been previously discovered by Portugal. There were many papal bulls which conferred upon Portugal sovereignty over the islands she had discovered and which we know today as the Cape Verde islands and that part of Africa lying east and south of the Cape Verde island.
When Columbus returned to Europe and showed that there was great promise of riches in the Indies the Portuguese were envious. The King and Queen of Spain wished to have confirmation of their claim to title and they advised Pope Alexander VI in the spring of 1493 that Columbus, sailing under the authority of Spain, had discovered the western islands en route to India. In May of 1493 Pope Alexander VI issued the two bulls granting sovereignty over one half of the unknown Western world to Spain and one half to Portugal.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on this subclause. I apologize to the committee for not realizing when I rose previously that we had stood subclause (d). I was saying at that time that the question of programming has exercised the minds of those in parliament for many years. There is a wide spectrum of opinion expressed with regard to this very contentious subject. At one end of the spectrum you have those who apparently hold the view that parliament should control C.B.C. television programming almost daily and pass opinion on every program as it appears. At the other end of the spectrum you have those who look upon broadcasting and those who engage in it as a group of sort of sacred cows. This group believes that parliament dare not express any opinion or offer any guide lines, in the interests of the Canadian people, to those responsible for broadcasting in this country.
I think that our responsibilities as elected members of parliament, representing all the Canadian people, is to put forward what we believe to be the interests of the Canadian people. We have a responsibility in this area, and in my mind there is no question about it. We have the responsibility to lay down guide lines and stake out conditions under which the Canadian people will be called upon to put up millions and millions of dollars every year in order to provide a national broadcasting service.
This may in some ways be a distasteful task, but it is one that we have to face. I commend the minister for her approach to this problem. If there is any doubt in one's

mind as to what our responsibilities might be, I think they are well expressed in the Fowler commission report at page 5, in the introduction. There, we find these words:
All broadcasting agencies-both public and private
are recipients of public support in the right to use scarce public assets. They must pay for these valuable rights by giving a responsible performance, and the state is fully entitled to ensure that the trust is honoured. To the extent that an adequate program performance is given voluntarily, the broadcaster can be left relatively free from detailed controls. If adequate performance is not given, it should be compelled by regulation or the franchise should be reassigned to others who will perform responsibly. Without question, the state has an absolute right to require from any broadcaster to whom the use of a radio frequency or television channel has been entrusted that he use it with imagination, distinction, and responsible regard for the public interest.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman, but I will not bore the committee by quoting further from the report. When hon. members speak of what is acceptable broadcasting to be received in the homes of Canadians by either radio or television, I would point out that there are some who immediately raise the cry of censorship and say that it conflicts with the principle of freedom of the press, freedom of speech and this sort of thing. I admit immediately that there is a vague resemblance, some similarity, between the problem with which we are trying to deal here and the principle of free speech. The two things are far from being identical, but they do have a similarity.
Their similarity is something like that which exists in the animal kingdom. The hyena has some similarity to the giraffe. They are both mammals, they each have fodr legs, and so forth. But the differences are perhaps greater than the similarities. I object, also, to the faulty reasoning put forward by those who raise the spectre of our impinging upon the right of free speech and come to the conclusion that because the giraffe is a tall animal, a high animal, he is really the hyena.
When we are discussing free speech I would point out that even with the free speech that is allowed at Hyde Park Comer in London, where there is free speech as we know it, there are certain limits beyond which one cannot go without running foul of the law of England. The right of free speech does not give people the right to slander or the right to abuse this privilege.
Quite often the freedom of broadcasting is compared with the freedom of the press. Here again, I do not think the comparison is on all fours. In the case of the press, which to begin with is a different medium, you may buy

I commend the minister and the government for making an attempt to draw up guide lines in this respect. This is a difficult job, no doubt. We should indicate somehow that broadcasters, just because they are broadcasters, are not above the law and that they have responsibilities to society; that it is not their prerogative to attack or to ridicule institutions which are part of the very fabric of our western way of life, to pollute our living rooms with all sorts of obscenities, or to glamorize for the consumption of young people the use of harmful drugs. The C.B.C. seems to have made an effort in this direction not so long ago. At one time they had the high priest of L.S.D. appearing on several programs, and, whether or not it was their intention, the effect was to glamorize the use of L.S.D. in the minds of the young people, if not of others.
It is some time since I was a member of the broadcasting committee. At that time television was just coming into use. Ever since people learned how to make fifes, the hearth has been the centre of the family home. People sat around it and conversed among themselves. But with the advent of television many families in this nation have been sitting around the "idiot box" instead of around the hearth and have been spoken to by people who set themselves up as leaders of thought. It does not matter how far out their thinking may be or how absurd it may be, what they say is given an aura of authority by the very fact that it is broadcast on the national, government-owned network provided by the government of Canada, presumably for the benefit of Canadians. It is for that reason I think it is important to set down guide lines.
Some of my friends to the left of me ask me whom I am trying to protect. I am not trying to protect anyone. I would be perfectly happy if there were some purely haphazard way in which differing points of view could be put forward on the national broadcasting system; if subjects could be picked at random and if those who supported them could go on the air as well as those who opposed them. I think that if there is a balanced presentation of various points of view the Canadian people

DEBATES	January 25, 1968
have sufficiently good judgment not to be carried away. However, what I object to is the apparent loss of control over this tremendously powerful medium and, either purposely or unintentionally, it seems to have fallen into the hands of a few people in the broadcasting industry who take it upon themselves to decide what is good for the Canadian people. Freedom of speech belongs to all citizens equally and is not the prerogative of the man with the microphone. However, the microphone gives him power to make his ideas known to millions and to drown out the ideas of those who do not agree with him because they are not given a chance to counter his views with their own opinions. Employees of the C.B.C. may hold any political ideas they like, but to propagate them on company time and at public expense over the public air waves is an injustice to their fellow citizens who do not have a great network over which to air their private ideas. It is almost as if an employee of the Royal Canadian Mint were given an opportunity to mint his own pocket money on the side. The whole idea is absurd. It is obvious that, as I have said already, we are purchasing a commodity at a cost of $150 million a year or more. The amount goes up so rapidly that I have lost track of it. It is important that we in parliament insist that the product we purchase is of reasonable quality. We should not attempt to censor any point of view but rather to guarantee that an objective presentation of the various points of view is made.
I should not like to leave the impression that I am anti-C.B.C. in all it does, because I am not. Let me say immediately that the C.B.C. has produced some excellent programs, such as, for example, "Country Calendar", "Fisherman's Log", some science programs, and even Don Messer's show, which is probably scorned by the producers of the C.B.C., or used to be at first. However, it has been listened to by more Canadians than any other program.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I think the C.B.C. does a magnificent job in many fields, but they spoil everything by their lax moral attitude, let alone their ethical attitude, as a result of which they purvey certain types of programs. Some people say: "Oh well, it is good for the Canadian people to be shocked; we have to shock them into reality". I do not go along with that opinion. I am not against shock treatment for those who are mentally ill, but I do not think that the general public needs it.
January 25. 1968

In an age when the great fight for survival is dependent on control over men's minds, it seems to me an anomaly that programs of the kind to which I have referred are broadcast. I am sure that control of men's minds is the real struggle today that is going to determine whether or not our civilization will survive.
Television broadcasting is a powerful weapon in such circumstances. Human beings have recently been described by an anthropologist in a book published on the subject as "hairless apes". His main theme is that we do not realize how much we are affected by emotions and how so little of what we do is determined rationally. Much of what we do is controlled by emotions, even though we kid ourselves into thinking that we are acting on a rational basis.

The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, who perhaps is more qualified on this subject than any other member in the house, pointed out in a very able speech on this question some months ago that we are still not really fully aware of the very great power that is inherent in television broadcasting in particular. We can be brain-washed, for example, without knowing it. We can also be influenced.
In the United Kingdom I believe there is a little society that contends that the world is flat. I am sure that if that little group were in Canada the C.B.C. would have them on one of their programs, which would probably be presented in this way. They would probably get a very fetching, bright looking young lady and a very photogenic young man who would speak on the side of the argument that the world was flat. They would then get some doddering old fellow, a Colonel Blimp type, who contended that the world was round.
In addition to this, Mr. Chairman, a sort of biography of this old fellow would be unfolded, and if they discovered that he had once almost belonged to the Klu Klux Klan, or something objectionable like that, this would be revealed so as to provide plenty of built-in
Canadian Policy on Broadcasting prejudice right from the start. In this way, without any reliance at all upon logic, they would have a few simple people believing that the world was flat after all. They would say: "How behind the times these squares are who still think that the world is round. Why, that is an old idea; it is a thousand years old. Let's get with it".
It is this kind of nonsense, Mr. Chairman, to which I object. As I have said, in this day and age when the struggle for men's minds is of crucial importance it is a terrible anomaly that we set the highest possible standards for our medical doctors, for the preparation of drugs and for anything to do with the human body, yet allow any sort of trash to be administered to the human mind.
My humble submission, Mr. Chairman, is that if we are going to provide a broadcasting service which will be relayed into the living rooms of the nation, then it should at least be housebroken. In this regard I refer especially to the C.B.C. The private broadcasters generally do better because if their service is too controversial they will not get a sponsor, and they do not want that to happen. But the C.B.C. apparently could not care less whether or not they have a sponsor for programs which deal with some of these far out notions, because the long suffering taxpayers are going to pick up the chit. These programs are shoved down our throats whether we like them or not. We just pay the bill. We cannot question the C.B.C. because it is a sacred cow. There is a prevailing attitude that parliament dare not question the C.B.C.
My contention is that a discussion of this clause is valid and of importance for one reason, if for no other. It is important in that it gives members of parliament a vehicle to express the views of the people they represent. I hope that the new president of the C.B.C. will take it as one of his first responsibilities to read what the members of parliament, the representatives of the people, think about broadcasting as it has been carried on in Canada. I believe that this important service for Canadians should, as I say, at least be housebroken before being allowed into the living room of every Canadian.

The standards of some of the programs produced by the C.B.C. I have no hesitation in saying, fall below accepted standards. They are a disgrace and should not be allowed on the Canadian air waves. This is particularly the case because, under some circumstances, we have no control over the programs which invade the parlour of our own home. It has been said that we can turn off the television set. We can do this if we are there, but with the complexities of life today we cannot always be there. Our children can turn on the set, and there is no monitor once a program comes on the air.
It has been said that we cannot do anything about this because the fat is in the fire. I think we can do something about it just on the basis of common sense. If these people put this type of program on the air, there must be an authority to inform them they will never do it again, and certainly not at the taxpayers' expense. If the hon. lady thinks that this job is too difficult for her, I suggest she should hand it over to somebody who has the normal courage of any free Canadian. At my age, I do not think seeing a filthy program will do me any particular harm. In my job as a policeman it was necessary for me on many occasions to delve into the lower side of human nature, yet I feel I have been able to maintain all my standards.
I do not believe this situation need be permanent, that we must face this with defeatism and say we cannot do anything about it. I believe here, in parliament, we can do everything about it. If these people knew that
January 25, 1968

their jobs depended upon cleaning up their own programs they would do so. I think the common sense of Canadians would come to the fore and these people would police themselves just as I did when I was a child because I knew the wrath that would descend upon me if I fell below our family standards. The family standards of the people of this country are well known. Anyone who does not have this type of common sense is not fit to produce programs.
If the hon. lady does not feel she has the power which I believe she has, then that power must be vested in someone. If Mr. Davidson does not have it then we must ask ourselves whether his assistant has it or whether anybody between the hon. lady who represents us and the man who produces the program has that power. There must be some authority somewhere. I do not intend to lay down any type of code except the code of common sense. We must give someone the power to police these programs, whether it is done before they are put on or afterward.
This subject, tied in with the question of abortion and the other changes to the Criminal Code, has been the cause of many, many letters and complaints. This is the thing most people are worried about today. I just answered this evening two letters on this subject. I told these people that I will do all I can. All I can do at the present time is try to convince enough members that we must be sure to put in this bill the teeth which are necessary to police the air waves of Canada. We can only do this through this bill and under the authority of the minister. I do not believe she should be afraid that people will accuse her of abusing her authority because she and no one else at the present time has any authority over the C.B.C. If she is willing to give us the authority to bring common sense into the matter of protecting our young people from some of the things shown on the Canadian air waves, she can rely on my support.

Mr. Chairman, we need state-ruled stations, because the state renders great services, but so does private enterprise.
In my opinion, private enterprise, competing with the state, is in a position to maintain programs, contribute to the education of the people, render great services at a lower cost than the state. Indeed, everything managed by the state costs three times more, and then some, than what is managed by private enterprise. We know the sums now spent by the state to maintain the C.B.C. I think that if these sums were in the hands of private enterprise, it would render greater services than the state, because the operating costs would certainly be reduced by half, if not by two thirds.
That is why private enterprise must be maintained as much as possible. Private enterprise renders greater services than the state, not only from the standpoint of publicity but from several others that I could mention. The small manufacturers and businessmen cannot advertise on C.B.C. but they can advertise on private stations and there set out their views and convince the people to help them to develop and expand Canada's economy.

That is where we must intervene. Several members referred to that matter and I wish to talk about it also. We should encourage morality, we should find a very deep ideology from a moral point of view to change the ethics of society, in short to rebuild society. Canadian Policy on Broadcasting In my opinion, it is the duty of the minister at the present time to ask the C.B.C. to improve the moral character of its programs and even to hire experts in ethics to show the people of Canada what is life, what is a human being.

Mr. Chairman, there is another aspect of subclause (d) with which I wish to deal. Subclauses (a) to (f) of clause 2 deal with broadcasting in general, both public and private, and subclause (g) deals with the national broadcasting service, or the C.B.C., in particular. I want to refer to one part of
[Mr. Latulippe.l
subclause (g) but I am using it in these remarks in connection with subclause (d).
Subclause (g) (iv) requires that the national broadcasting service, the C.B.C., should contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity. This is a charge upon the public broadcasting service only. When the bill was given second reading on November 1 I expressed some doubts about the words in this subclause charging the public broadcasting service to contribute to the development of national unity. I did not do so because I am against national unity any more than anyone else, but the opportunity is there for witch-hunting and for picking out people in a broadcasting service who you feel are not doing what you want them to do. After listening to the speeches in the house on this subject, I have come to the conclusion that the opportunities for witch-hunting will certainly be there. But the government apparently wants this provision in the bill, and it occurred to me that if the concept of national unity is so important and broadcasters should contribute to it, it ought to be a requirement in respect of all broadcasters. It is a very vague term and is very difficult to define but if, as I say, the government wants it included in the bill it should be important enough to be a guide for all broadcasters.
There are in this country more private television and radio stations than there are C.B.C. stations. Therefore, it seems to me that if television and radio can be used to influence the way people think and act, the private broadcasters also have, of course, a very great deal of influence. If this charge to contribute to national unity is necessary, it should, I believe, be included in subclause (d), for two reasons; first of all, because it fits in better there in connection with the requirement to air views on matters of public controversy and to allow for dissent.
The second reason, which I have already mentioned, is that the private broadcasters have a very large audience. I thought of this matter the other day when there was an exchange between the hon. member for La-to the hon. member the minister had this to pointe and the minister. The hon. member for Lapointe was talking about the television station in Quebec city, CFCM-TV. In her reply say, as reported at page 5814 of Hansard for January 22:
I am further informed by Television de Quebec that their editorial policy favours freedom as against communism, private enterprise as against socialism and Canadian unity as against separatism.
January 25, 1968
COMMONS DEBATES	5991
Presumably the operators of that station are in the same position as the owners of a newspaper; they can, entirely on their own, determine what is their editorial policy. Therefore, if they choose to promote a particular line of thought, that is their editorial right. But what would happen if that station should change hands? Let us suppose that the hon. member for Lapointe, on one of his trips to France, raised enough money to buy that station and had complete control of it. Then, presumably the editorial policy of the station could change in accordance with the views of the new owner. It could then decide that separatism should be the editorial policy of the station rather than Canadian unity. I do not imagine that the hon. member for Lapointe would advocate socialism rather than private enterprise, but he could do so if he wished, since he would be the owner of the station. He could do any of these things.
I have had some experience in this field and know that radio stations regularly editorialize. I do not complain about that; they are free to do this. If my hon. friend from Lapointe, or somebody else with his views, owned such a station, they could advocate disunity. We will not confine our examples to the province of Quebec entirely. There is another province of Canada which has a rather separatist-leaning government. I refer to the province from which I come. More than one cabinet member in that province has suggested that Canada should join the United States. Yes, I am speaking of British Columbia. If people with that point of view bought a radio station, they could editorialize and suggest that we no longer remain in confederation but join the United States. This obviously would not be promoting national unity.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am suggesting that if broadcasters are to promote national unity, all broadcasters should do this, both public and private, and this particular phrase should be included in subclause (d). With that in mind, I move:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I speak tonight following a question asked on December 14 in which I requested the Department of National Health and Welfare to strengthen its staff for the collection of D.B.S. statistics and to provide additional resources so that the staff could be increased for the collation of statistics. The question on December 14 was prompted by a reply to a written question on December 13 which appears at page 5363 of Hansard. In the answer, we learn that in the health and welfare division of D.B.S. there are some 105 persons involved in collecting statistics relating to health, some 31 persons occupied in collecting statistics relating to education, but no persons directly involved with statistics concerning welfare. When we keep in mind that the Department of National Health and Welfare is second in spending only to the department of defence, it seems surprising to me that there is no statistical documentation of the different trends toward which this high spending department is going so far as welfare programs are concerned.
Fabulous sums of money are being spent on a variety of welfare programs, yet adequate statistics are not being kept to determine the cost benefit to the Canadian people. Welfare budgets have doubled and re-doubled and will likely continue to increase, and it is certainly difficult to make any projections without an adequate statistical base. I would have thought that the implementation of the Canada Assistance Plan would have required the collection of national welfare items of similarity, but the dilemma still facing those of us interested in finding similar information relating to welfare in the different provinces is that there is a great variety of methodology in the collecting of statistics. For example, the province of Ontario has quite a sophisticated system of statistical analysis, and yet areas like the Atlantic regions and other provinces do not nearly approach this way of collecting statistics. Therefore, it is not easy to discover how many married people in Canada are, for example, living separately.
5992	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
As we deal in our present legislative program with what the Prime Minister called "good society" measures, such as those on divorce, birth control, abortion and so forth, some of these statistics would have been very useful. We do not really know how many people there are in the country who have sig-significant family problems. We can go from agency to agency and from province to province but we do not have an overall national picture. If I wanted, I could inquire of D.B.S. and get fairly accurate information concerning the number of ponies on Sable island or the total horse population in Canada, but we cannot find out how many children are living in foster homes or are placed in adoption each year. To me this seems to indicate a desperate lack in the collection of very vital information.
In the area of child care, I have mentioned already the problem of obtaining accurate statistics with regard to children living and growing up away from their natural parents, either in foster homes or in child care institutions. We should be able to ascertain those things by requesting our most capable organization, the D.B.S., to collate the information. It could do this. First of all, it could give us the information and second, this would force provincial governments to set up a uniform base for the collection of statistics.
I am not one who wishes to collect information simply to pile up figures. This should only be done for a purpose. We are now quite conscious of the need for research, for example. I am afraid that very often we are stymied in our research in the welfare field owing to the lack of statistics. Generally, we find ourselves taking 10 per cent of United States figures, the United States usually documenting its research quite well, and we adopt this figure as being fairly close to the situation in Canada. However, I suggest that is not an adequate foundation upon which to conduct proper research.
My direct question, Mr. Speaker, is simply this: Will the department strengthen its staff for the collection of welfare and related statistics and allocate additional resources and staff to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics?
