speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) what plans his department had for the promotion and development of secondary and manufacturing industry in
January 25, 1968
COMMONS DEBATES	5993
British Columbia, which is now in the position of having something over 6 per cent of the labour force out of work, the second highest group in Canada.
The minister replied that to recite the steps that are being taken would take too long during the question period but that he would be glad to advise me directly about this matter. I was not sure what he meant by "directly" and I have been expecting a long, detailed letter from him; but this letter has not yet arrived. If the minister wants to deal with the matter in this way and the three minutes that remain for him this evening are not sufficient, then I will look forward to receiving his letter. Apart from the fact that his answer was in a gentle way political and also somewhat arrogant, none the less his department was established partly for the purpose of promoting industrial development in Canada.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We in British Columbia, and particularly in the northwestern area of Skeena which encompasses nearly all the northwestern section of British Columbia, enjoy an economy that is primarily based on the extraction of natural resources. Most of our industry is of the extractive type and much of the natural wealth which we obtain from our land is shipped out of the area, often out of the country, to be used in secondary or manufacturing industries elsewhere.
We have a fair amount of mineral wealth, timber and power in the form of coal and hydroelectric power. We have much potential power. The opportunities for secondary and manufacturing industry in the area are tremendous.
It is well known that human labour adds to the value of any material to which it is applied. The raw ore which comes out of the ground is not as valuable as the ore which has gone through a concentrating process. Raw concentrate is not as valuable as concentrate which has gone through a smelter and been turned into ingots. At every stage of manufacturing process value is added to raw material. We wish to promote secondary and manufacturing industries in our area which will take advantage of our raw materials and natural resources.
There is ample opportunity for the development of a smelter system in the area. At the moment, largely as a result of this government's insistence and its declarations of policy, we export the mineral resources of our area out of our nation to another country and contribute to the increasingly high standard
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of living of that other country. I shall mention no names because it may be thought that I object to another country's increasing standard of living, an increasing standard made possible by the raw materials we export to it 1 do object to our government permitting that state of affairs.
We could easily establish a secondary aluminum industry in the area; we already have an aluminum smelter. No facilities for transforming aluminum ingots into sheets, tubes, pipes or other manufactured forms of aluminum exist. Ample opportunities for such industries to operate successfully exist in the area.
Similar remarks apply to the forest industry. Many examples of the sort of thing I mentioned could be enumerated. Because the Department of Industry was set up to promote industrial development in areas in Canada which could use that sort of development, and because parliament accepted the proposition that a Department of Industry ought to be set up, I submit that something concrete and worth while along the lines I have suggested ought to be undertaken.
Though the minister, under the rules, has only a few moments to reply, I hope that he can explain what he has done, what is taking place and what plans exist, so that the people in northwestern British Columbia whose employment opportunities fluctuate according to the weather and other factors can look forward with some hope to the time when something such as I have described, some smelting industry or some manufacturing industry based on lumber or aluminum, can be made a reality. It is necessary for our people to have some hope, and I should appreciate some guidance from the minister.

To this end we have a number of programs which have been discussed and approved by parliament. I would mention specifically the program for the advancement of industrial technology designed to increase productivity and economy in manufacturing in all of Canada. The act providing incentives to increased research and development is of a similar character and is nationwide.
With respect to British Columbia specifically, there is a program devoted directly to the relief of areas of chronic unemployment. This is known as the designated areas program and those areas of British Columbia which suffer from high chronic unemployment have been designated under this plan. In the south central part of the province where this program has been in operation it has proved
reasonably successful. There has been a total of some 53 projects involving new capital investment of some $50 million in secondary, manufacturing or processing industries. This has resulted in the creation of some 1,755 new jobs.
This is the one overall program which is directed specifically to a particular area as distinct from Canada as a whole. I would point out that we have been conducting a series of seminars among entrepreneurs and manufacturers across the country looking toward an improvement in efficiency and the enlargement of manufacturing industry. I myself attended a most successful recent one in Vancouver.

Government of Newfoundland and Labrador THE PREMIER St. John's
2 January, 1968
Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, P.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
My dear Prime Minister:
Thank you so much for your letter about the Constitutional Conference, which I acknowledge in the Premier's absence.
My Colleagues and I would be delighted to have one or two of your representatives come to St. John's for a preliminary exchange of views on the Conference. I would hope that they could meet with the Premier, and also I think they should get in touch with my Colleague the Minister of Justice, the Hon. T. A. Hickman, and with the Premier's Parliamentary Assistant, Edward Roberts.
Sincerely yours,
L. R. Curtis, Acting Premier.
December 28, 1967
My dear Premier:
Our preparations for the Constitutional Conference of early February are now in progress and I hope to be in a position to send you some background papers in the near future.
I believe that it would be very worthwhile if one or two of my representatives were to meet with you in your Capital during the month of January for a preliminary exchange of views, and to note any suggestions you may wish to offer concerning the matters on the agenda of the conference, or its procedure. In addition to other talks they may have with your officials, and other Ministers if you so wish, I think it would be very helpful if they could also meet with you personally.
I would suggest the date of February 1 for such a meeting, if this is convenient to you.
Yours sincerely,
Original signed by
L. B. Pearson
The Honourable J. R. Smallwood,
Premier of Newfoundland,
St. John's, Newfoundland.

My dear Prime Minister:

Nova Scotia THE PREMIER Halifax
December 7, 1967
CONFIDENTIAL Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
This will acknowledge yours of December 1st with reference to a Federal-Provincial Conference to consider establishing a constitutional Bill of Rights. I would be prepared to attend on Monday, February 5th, and to continue on the following day, and as required further.
It seems to me that there are really two problems which tend to make many millions of Canadians very unhappy.
One, of course, is that of language and culture.
The other question is that of disparity in regional development. If we are going to tackle one we should at the same time and with the same degree of anxiety tackle the other. It therefore seems to me that it would be appropriate to place on the agenda of the proposed meeting the whole question of regional disparity.
Sincerely yours,
G. I. Smith

Toronto, Ontario, December 6, 1967 Confidential
My dear Prime Minister;
Monday, February 5th, is agreeable to Ontario as the day on which the Federal-Provincial Conference might be convened next year to deal with various constitutional matters. We will also be ready to discuss the Report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism.
In regard to making some of the sessions public, I think that this should be given a great deal of careful consideration. Certainly in the context of bringing our people to realize the gravity of our discussions and perhaps the divergence of points of view, some public
sessions would seem to be indicated. On the other hand, we must never lose sight of the fact that the decision making process is not helped or made easier when carried on in the white glare of publicity. I have always been of the opinion that there is a happy medium to be followed.
My suggestion would be that we give some consideration to dealing with some general subjects in the early stages of the Conference, where points of view might be put, with the latter part of the Conference held in camera. This could be done quite easily by a close examination of the agenda and by its proper arrangement to meet these requirements.
I would be happy to discuss this with you when we next meet.
Yours sincerely,
John P. Rob arts
Right Honourable L. B. Pearson,

My dear Prime Minister:
Thank you for your letter of the 1st and particularly for your kind good wishes on my taking office as Premier of Manitoba and leader of the Manitoba Progressive Conservative Party.
I have consulted my Cabinet colleagues and can inform you that the suggested dates for the federal-provincial conference beginning Monday, February 5, 1968, are satisfactory to the Manitoba government. I have noted what you say regarding the agenda of the conference and will certainly write to you in due course to suggest any related matters which might be added to it.
In view of the experience gained at the Confederation of Tomorrow Conference in Toronto last week, you might consider having the opening meeting of the federal-provincial conference in February open to the public and to the news media including television. In this way the position papers set forth by the representatives of the Government of Canada and of the various provinces would be made known to the widest possible public. Whether

Ottawa, December 1, 1967.
My dear Premier:
You will recall that I wrote you on August 15th proposing that a Federal-Provincial Conference be convened early next year to consider the possibility of establishing a constitutional Bill of Rights for Canada. All provinces have now responded and expressed general willingness to participate. It would be helpful for planning purposes if we could now agree on a possible date for our meeting.
I should like to suggest that the Conference might begin on Monday, February 5, with the intention of continuing the discussion on the following day and, if need be, on Wednesday. I would appreciate if you could let me know as soon as possible whether this suggested date is suitable to you.
In so far as the agenda of the Conference is concerned, our intention, as you know, is to focus discussion on a constitutional Bill of Rights. Since our original proposal, we have received the Report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism which will be made public next week, a copy of which will be sent to you. I think we should provide some time for a discussion of the Report and its recommendations. In addition, the Provincial Governments have also now had an opportunity to have some discussions between

I would also appreciate your views as to whether or not some of the sessions should be made public, bearing in mind of course that our discussions may eventually lead to decisions by both levels of government.
Yours sincerely,
